article.overview: An ice detection radar is a radar instrument intended to find water ice on or beneath the surface of a planetary body. Radar sends radio or microwave signals toward the ground and records the returning echoes. Ice, regolith and rock return different echoes, so the strength, polarisation and delay of the returns can be used to infer what material is present. On the Moon, the main interest is water ice in permanently shadowed craters near the poles. The catalogue entry 'Ice detection radar' is a class name, not a single named instrument. This article therefore describes the general concept, three flown radars with lunar ice-related objectives (Mini-SAR on Chandrayaan-1 [3][8], Mini-RF on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter [4][5] and DFSAR on Chandrayaan-2 [2][6]) and the evidence gaps. It does not assert a single design, mass or performance for the class.
article.description: A radar-based ice detector generally has four functional parts: (1) a transmitter producing microwave or radio pulses or a continuous signal at one or more wavelengths; (2) an antenna that directs the signal toward the surface and collects returning echoes, where synthetic aperture radar (SAR) designs combine echoes from many positions along the spacecraft track to form a higher-resolution image; (3) a receiver and digitiser that records amplitude, phase and, where the design allows, polarisation of the returns; and (4) a processing chain that converts raw echoes into maps or profiles, which scientists interpret using echo polarisation properties and comparisons with other data sets such as neutron spectroscopy and illumination maps. The three flown examples below use these parts with different choices of frequency, polarisation and antenna.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of an ice-detection radar is to map where water ice may exist and to distinguish it from other forms of lunar water. Mini-SAR was built to detect water ice in the permanently shadowed polar regions, and it reported high circular polarisation ratio (CPR) signatures inside some polar craters that were absent outside their rims [3][1]. Mini-RF's primary science objective was to search for water-ice deposits in the permanently shadowed areas of the north and south polar regions [4]. DFSAR data have been used to examine doubly shadowed craters inside the south-polar permanently shadowed regions for signs of subsurface ice [2]. Radar can in principle probe below the surface. ISRO states that Mini-SAR could detect ice up to a depth of a few metres [3]; the depth reached by Mini-RF and DFSAR was not verified in this article.
article.operating_principle: Radar detects a target by transmitting a signal and measuring its echo. For ice detection, the most important echo properties are: dielectric contrast, because materials with different electrical properties reflect and transmit radio waves differently and water ice behaves differently from dry regolith; polarisation, because the polarisation of the returned signal can change with surface and subsurface structure; and roughness and volume scattering, because surface roughness, rocks and buried structure also scatter radar energy and can imitate or mask an ice signal. The circular polarisation ratio (CPR) is the ratio of same-sense to opposite-sense returns for a circularly polarised transmission. Mini-SAR transmits left-circularly polarised pulses, and most surfaces return mainly right-circular echoes; high CPR can arise from very rough, fresh surfaces or from ice [1]. NASA states that CPR is 'not uniquely diagnostic of either roughness or ice' [1]. Mini-RF uses a hybrid-polarimetric mode with circular transmit and linear horizontal and vertical receive [4]. The 2026 DFSAR criterion uses CPR greater than 1 together with a degree of polarisation below 0.13 as an indicator of volumetric scattering that may come from subsurface ice [2]. These principles are standard in radar science. The numerical thresholds used to identify ice in Mini-SAR and Mini-RF data are not established in this article beyond the values cited here.
article.scientific_importance: The Moon's polar ice is scientifically and operationally important. NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter mission page states that LRO is helping NASA identify areas near the Moon's South Pole with crucial resources such as water [10]. Radar is one of several methods used to investigate this question. It sees the surface from above and is sensitive to material properties, so it provides information complementary to neutron, reflectance and thermal measurements. As an example of cross-checking, NASA compared Mini-SAR's ice estimate with a Lunar Prospector neutron estimate of several hundred million metric tons, while noting that the neutron instrument probes only about half a metre deep and may undercount [1]. The strength of any single radar result depends on whether its interpretation is confirmed by other data, and that confirmation has not been established for any specific deposit in this article.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for an ice-detection radar. Mass, dimensions, power, frequency and resolution depend strongly on the instrument design and mission. The three examples below are flown instruments with different designs, so the comparison is only loose.

examples.name: Mini-SAR (Miniature Synthetic Aperture Radar) on Chandrayaan-1
examples.type: Flown lunar orbital imaging radar (single frequency, hybrid polarity)
examples.host_spacecraft: ISRO Chandrayaan-1 orbiter; NASA describes Mini-SAR as one of 11 instruments on that mission [1].
examples.description_of_role: Built to detect water ice in the permanently shadowed polar regions. NASA reported high-CPR craters interpreted as consistent with water ice [1][3].
frequency_bands: S-band, 2.38 GHz (ISRO); wavelength not stated by ISRO
examples.resolution: 75 m per pixel from a 100 km orbit (ISRO).
examples.mass_description: 8.77 kg as stated by ISRO [3]. NASA describes the instrument as less than 10 kg [1]. An antenna mass of 3.3 kg appears in a Current Science table read from a search snippet [8].
examples.antenna_type: Not described in the sources accessed.
examples.dimensions: Not stated in the sources accessed.
examples.operational_status: Orbit raised to 200 km in May 2009; communication lost on 29 August 2009 (ISRO [3]).
examples.qualification: Frequency, mass and resolution from the ISRO page [3]. The antenna mass is from a search-indexed table that was not read in full [8]. Power was not located.

examples.name: Mini-RF (Miniature Radio Frequency instrument) on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
examples.type: Flown lunar orbital synthetic aperture radar (technology demonstration and extended-mission science instrument)
examples.description_of_role: Primary science objective: search for water-ice deposits in permanently shadowed areas of the north and south polar regions [4].
examples.resolution: Baseline 150 m at 16 looks; zoom 15 m by 30 m at 8 looks [4]. The 2010 summary gives 150 m and 30 m [5].
examples.mass_description: 15-kg class instrument according to the PDS catalogue [4]. The 2010 summary describes a 16 kg package [5]. Exact mass not stated.
examples.antenna_type: Passive array of horizontal and vertical elements, about 1 square metre [4].
examples.dimensions: Not stated in the sources accessed.
examples.launch_date: Not stated in the PDS file [4].
examples.operational_status: A Wikipedia summary reports a transmitter critical failure in January 2011, after the primary objectives were met, with the receiver still supporting occasional bistatic measurements. Not confirmed against NASA [9].
examples.qualification: Band wavelengths and resolution from the PDS catalogue [4]. The Wikipedia values of 12.6 cm and 4.2 cm [9] differ slightly and are not used. Findings by Spudis et al. (2013) are from the abstract record only [7].

examples.name: DFSAR (Dual-Frequency Synthetic Aperture Radar) on Chandrayaan-2
examples.type: Flown lunar orbital synthetic aperture radar (L-band and S-band, fully polarimetric)
examples.description_of_role: ISRO describes DFSAR as the first fully polarimetric SAR used to study the Moon. It was used in 2026 for a subsurface-ice study of doubly shadowed craters [2].
examples.resolution: Not stated in the sources accessed.
examples.mass_description: About 20 kg, as reported on the arXiv abstract page [6]. The full paper was not retrieved.
examples.antenna_type: Not stated in the sources accessed.
examples.dimensions: Not stated in the sources accessed.
examples.launch_date: Not stated in the sources accessed.
examples.operational_status: Preliminary on-orbit calibration matched pre-launch expected values (arXiv abstract [6]). The 2026 subsurface-ice result is reported by ISRO [2].
examples.qualification: The 2026 criterion (CPR above 1 and degree of polarisation below 0.13) is from ISRO [2]. The Sinha et al. paper was not opened. A preprint disputes the roughness interpretation [11].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Not publicly specified for a generic ice-detection radar. Dimensions were not stated for Mini-SAR, Mini-RF or DFSAR in the sources accessed.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Not publicly specified for a generic ice-detection radar. Flown examples: Mini-SAR 8.77 kg (ISRO); Mini-RF 15-kg class (PDS); DFSAR about 20 kg (arXiv abstract page). These figures describe different instruments and should not be compared as if they were the same design.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified for a generic ice-detection radar. Power was not located for Mini-SAR, Mini-RF or DFSAR in the sources accessed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar ice-detection radar must function in vacuum, under wide temperature swings and under radiation. Polar craters add the difficulty of very low temperatures and long periods without direct sunlight. ISRO describes the doubly shadowed craters studied for DFSAR as very cold, at around 25 K [2]. Engineering requirements not verified for any specific instrument include thermal control, radiation tolerance, pointing knowledge and data-downlink capacity. For an orbiting radar, orbital geometry, look angle and the ability to observe shadowed regions are important operational factors. Mini-RF's SAR observations were made over selected sites poleward of plus or minus 80 degrees latitude without interfering with LRO's primary instruments [4].
article.limitations: Radar echoes are sensitive to surface roughness, rock content and buried structure, which can produce false or ambiguous ice signatures. Spatial resolution sets the smallest resolvable feature. The Mini-SAR figure of 75 m per pixel and the Mini-RF baseline of 150 m are much coarser than the scale of individual ice grains or thin layers [3][4]. A single measurement cannot establish the amount or depth of ice without independent data, and both the Mini-SAR volume estimate and the DFSAR criterion have been questioned in the literature [1][11]. Mini-RF's transmitter failure, reported in January 2011, limited its later use [9].

transportation_and_deployment.overview: All three flown examples were orbiter payloads. No surface ice-detection radar was verified in this article.
transportation_process: Integrate the radar into the host spacecraft on Earth.
Launch the spacecraft on a launch vehicle (Mini-SAR launched on Chandrayaan-1 on 22 October 2008 [3]).
Transfer the spacecraft to the Moon.
Insert the spacecraft into lunar orbit.
Commission the radar, including pointing, thermal and data-interface checks.
For a surface radar (not verified in this article): deploy and mount the antenna, connect power, thermal and data interfaces, and assess how the surface environment affects returns.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Not applicable to the three flown examples, which were orbiter payloads. Mini-RF was carried on LRO [4][5]. DFSAR is carried by the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter [2]. The integration and commissioning steps for these instruments were not verified in this article. No surface deployment method for an ice-detection radar was verified.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Mini-SAR on Chandrayaan-1 [3], Mini-RF on LRO [4][5] and DFSAR on Chandrayaan-2 [2] are the flown examples described in this article.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a named lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted. Compatibility would require verified mass, dimensions, mounting, power, thermal and data-interface specifications.

article.historical_significance: Mini-SAR on Chandrayaan-1 reported high-CPR signatures interpreted as possible polar water ice, and NASA published its account in March 2010 while the findings were being prepared for Geophysical Research Letters [1]. Mini-RF on LRO was built to demonstrate a lightweight SAR and to search for polar water ice [4][5]. DFSAR on Chandrayaan-2 is the most recent of the three, and in 2026 it was used for a subsurface-ice study of doubly shadowed craters [2]. Together these radars form the main radar evidence for polar ice. That evidence remains debated, and the Mini-RF and DFSAR interpretations are both contested in the literature [7][11].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: 'Ice detection radar' is a class name; no single design, mass, power, frequency range or lifetime can be assigned to the class. Mini-SAR's frequency and mass come from the ISRO page, but its antenna mass comes from a search-indexed table and its full instrument table was not read. Mini-RF's band wavelengths come from the PDS catalogue, while its 30 m zoom resolution and transmitter failure come from secondary summaries. The Spudis et al. (2013) and later Mini-RF analyses were read only at abstract level or from search summaries. DFSAR's mass comes from an arXiv abstract page and its full paper was not retrieved. The 2026 DFSAR subsurface-ice result is reported by ISRO, the crater count differs between sources, and a preprint disputes the roughness interpretation. Power for all three instruments was not located. No direct image asset was verified in this version. No lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility was assessed.

image_handling.url_policy: All URL values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. No image URLs were added because no direct image asset was verified in this version.

data_quality_notes: v2 adds research from primary agency pages (ISRO for Mini-SAR and DFSAR, NASA PDS for Mini-RF), an arXiv abstract for DFSAR, and abstract-level or search-summary records for Mini-RF and Mini-SAR. Full papers for Spudis et al. (2013), Nozette et al. (2010), Sinha et al. (2026) and the Current Science Mini-SAR paper were not read in full.

Correction to v1: Mini-RF resolution is given in the PDS catalogue as a 150 m baseline and a 15 m by 30 m zoom mode. The v1 value of 30 m per pixel was one of these modes, not a general figure. Band wavelengths are taken from the PDS catalogue (12 cm and 4 cm), not the Wikipedia values (12.6 cm and 4.2 cm) used in v1.
Mini-RF mass is given as a 15-kg class instrument in the PDS catalogue and as a 16 kg package in the 2010 summary. Exact mass was not established.

Mini-SAR mass: 8.77 kg from ISRO. NASA gives less than 10 kg. A search snippet of a 2010 EPSC abstract gives about 8 kg. An antenna mass of 3.3 kg is listed in a Current Science table seen only in a search snippet. These values were not reconciled.
DFSAR mass of about 20 kg comes from an arXiv abstract page and has not been checked against the full paper. Resolution, power and orbit values for DFSAR were not verified.

The Mini-SAR volume estimate (600 million metric tons, also given by NASA as 600 million cubic metres) rests on a unit equivalence stated in the NASA caption. This is a source assumption, not a measured quantity.

The 2026 DFSAR subsurface-ice result is reported by ISRO and cites Sinha et al. in npj Space Exploration, which was not opened. ISRO's text describes four craters; press reports describe nine. A Research Square preprint argues that roughness can explain the enhanced CPR. The preprint has not been peer reviewed.

The Mini-RF transmitter failure in January 2011 is from a Wikipedia summary and has not been confirmed against NASA. The Cabeus bistatic result and the claim that Mini-RF CPR correlates with rock abundance come from search summaries only and are not used as established findings.
No image was verified as a direct asset from an official source page in this version. Image arrays are empty and no image_url values are populated.
No lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility is asserted. Transportation discussion is generic and orbiter-based for the three flown examples.
